newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua presidential race tightens - poll.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua presidential race tightens - poll.

text.p: Former President Daniel Ortega of the leftist Sandinista Front has pulled to within four percentage points of right-wing rival Arnoldo Aleman in the lastest poll in Nicaragua's presidential race.

The CID-Gallup poll showed Aleman of the Liberal Alliance with 34 percent of the vote and Ortega with 30 percent, followed by 21 other candidates, none of whom received more than 2.4 percent. The margin of error was 2.7 percent.
The competing Borge y Asociados poll in August gave Aleman a 10-percentage-point lead over Ortega heading into Nicaragua's Oct. 20 presidential elections.

"The main trend is the rise of the Sandinistas. Daniel Ortega's popularity has risen by nine percent since April," said Carlos Denton, president of CID-Gallup in Costa Rica, on the morning talk show Buenos Dias on Thursday.
In contrast, Aleman's popularity had fallen by two percent since then, he said.
The poll suggested the election would go to a second round, since neither candidate was likely to get the 45 percent needed to win in the first round.
Denton attributed the rise in Ortega's popularity to Nicaragua's economic crisis, which has left 54 percent of the work force either unemployed or under-employed.
Among those surveyed who said their economic situation was worse this year than last year, Ortega out-polled Aleman.
"When all is said and done, people vote with their stomach, and right now the people are suffering," Denton said.
The poor and unemployed were starting to see Ortega as the candidate who could get them jobs and food, Denton added.
Two-thirds of those polled said unemployment was the most important election issue.
The poll also showed that many Nicaraguans still had little faith in their democratic process, with 48.4 percent saying election fraud was a possibility in their district.
The Sandinistas governed Nicaragua from 1979 to 1990, maintaining close ties with the Soviet Union and Cuba, while fighting an eight-year war against U.S.-backed Contra rebels.
